title: TB8-18843
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX (the Minor Appellant), are citizens of China. They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellants alleged before the RPD that the Principal Appellant was forced to have tubal ligation after the birth of her second child in 2008. Her life was deeply affected by this. She was introduced to Church of Almighty God by a friend in early 2017 and she began to attend church meetings at a sister's home. On July 28, 2017 she was informed by her church leader that a fellow church leader and some members had been arrested. She was advised to go into hiding. The Appellants already had visitors' visas for Canada and flew to Toronto XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. They were told by the Principal Appellant's mother-in-law on August 9, 2017 that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) had searched for her at the family home and were aware that she was a member of the Almighty God underground church. The PSB informed the mother-in-law that they had already arrested the leader of her group, as well as other members and that none had been released.

The Appellants' claim for refugee protection was heard on May 28, 2018. In a written decision signed on July 3, 2018, the RPD rejected their claim finding the Principal Appellant had not established on a balance of probabilities, that she was a genuine practitioner of the Almighty God faith either in China or in Canada, and that she would not practice that faith should she return to China. The RPD extended those findings to the Minor Appellant's claim.
The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its credibility findings and by not conducting a sur place analysis. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Credibility Group Practice Location in China

The RPD took a negative credibility inference from the Principal Appellant's inability to identify where her group's Almighty God gatherings were located in China. The RPD found that her evidence that the locations were secret and that she had forgotten the locations was confusing, vague and contradictory.
The Appellants argue that the Principal Appellant offered a reasonable explanation which should have been accepted by the RPD.

The RAD has reviewed the record and has listened to the recording of the hearing. The RAD agrees with the RPD that the Principal Appellant's testimony in regard to where her group practiced was confusing and internally inconsistent. The RAD notes that several questions had to be asked in order to acquire testimony about the Principal Appellant's meeting location. She was first asked where the meetings were held and she replied that it was at a sister's home. She was asked where that was and she replied in China. She was again asked where that was and she replied it was a country area. She was asked to be more specific and she replied that it was in Changle city. She was asked for the location and she replied the address was secret at the time and she could not state the name. She later stated that she had known the location, but had forgotten it because it had been a while ago. The RAD notes that the Principal Appellant testified at the hearing that she began to go to church meetings in early 2017 and attended 1 to 2 times per week until the end of July 2017, for a period of approximately six months. The RAD has considered that there is no evidence in the record regarding any memory issues suffered by the Principal Appellant and finds that her testimony about where she practiced her religion in China was evasive and evolving. Furthermore, the RAD finds that details about where her church group met go to the heart of her claim that she began to practice the Almighty God faith in China and the RAD takes a negative credibility inference from the lack of detail about her meeting location and the internal inconsistencies in her evidence. Knowledge and practice in Canada

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Principal Appellant does not practice the Almighty God faith in Canada given that she had not made reasonable efforts to explore and inquire about the practice of the faith in Canada. The RPD considered that she did not practice her faith with a group and relied only on the website because she had been advised that there was no gathering spot in Canada. The RPD found that her testimony about how she practices in Canada was vague and without detail.

The RPD found that the Principal Appellant did not have basic or fundamental understanding of the Almighty God faith. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant testified that she believes in the Trinity and explained what that was; whereas the documentary evidence indicates that one of the core teachings of the church of Almighty God is that the Trinity is a false doctrine and that instead, one God simply used different names in the three different ages. The RPD considered that the Principal Appellant had been practicing the faith since February 2017, and that it was reasonable to expect her to understand of the core teachings and belief of the faith. The RPD made a negative credibility inference and found that the Principal Appellant did not practice the faith either in Canada or China.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to appreciate that it is noted in the documentary evidence that scholars of religion often observe that Chinese believers tend to believe in whatever is efficacious, are not concerned about the finer points of doctrine/Scripture and many adherents are reported to have a low level of literacy. They submit that the RPD's benchmark for Almighty God knowledge was set too high and that the RPD expected the Principal Appellant to have encyclopedic knowledge of the principles of the church of Almighty God. They argue that the RPD erred by dismissing the Principal Appellant's knowledge of the principles of the church of Almighty God as basic and further erred by failing to explain what standards of knowledge it was measuring against.

The RAD has reviewed the record and finds that the RPD did not err by taking a negative credibility inference from the Principal Appellant's belief in the Trinity, which is inconsistent with the fundamental teachings of her religion. The RAD notes that the country conditions documentary evidence explicitly states that the core teaching of the Church of Almighty God is that the Trinity is a false doctrine.1 Given that this is the core teaching, and not one of the finer points, the RAD does not find that the RPD set the benchmark too high for the knowledge expected of the Principal Appellant regarding her religion. The RAD notes that at the hearing in May 2018 the Principal Appellant testified that she practiced this religion for approximately six months while in China, attending group services 1 to 2 times per week and that she has been accessing the Church of Almighty God website online since coming to Canada in XXXX 2017. At the hearing she was asked whether she believed in the Trinity and she replied that she believed. She was asked to describe what the Trinity was and she stated that it was the Holy Father, Son and Spirit. She was asked again whether she believed in the Trinity and again she replied that she believed. The RAD notes that there is no evidence in the record that the Principal Appellant had ever practiced any other form of Christianity and the source of her belief in the Trinity is therefore unclear.

While the RAD is aware that it is not necessary for a claimant to exhibit microscopic knowledge of her religion, in this particular case, it was a core belief of the Church of Almighty God doctrine that the Principal Appellant was unaware of. The RAD notes that at the time of the hearing in May 2018 the Principal Appellant had already been practicing this religion for approximately one and 1/2 years. There is no evidence in the record that her cognitive functions were impaired in any way and the RAD notes that that she has eight years of formal education and had worked in China as a financial executive for 12 years.2 The RAD finds, given her personal circumstances, it is reasonable to expect that she would have some knowledge of the core teaching of the religion she professes to follow. The RAD disagrees with the Appellants' argument this was peripheral knowledge that does not go to the root of her practice as it is very clearly stated in the country conditions documentary evidence that the core belief of the religion is that the Trinity is a false doctrine. The RAD notes that the Principal Appellant's most recent practice of her religion involved reading the materials on the church's website and finds that she has demonstrated that she has a sufficiently high level of literacy in order to access these materials. The RAD finds that the RPD did not err in its assessment of the Principal Appellant's religious knowledge.

The RAD has additionally considered the RPD finding that the Principal Appellant's testimony about how she practices her religion in Canada was vague and without detail. The RAD has reviewed the record and agrees with the RPD that the testimony provided by the Principal Appellant in this regard was sparse, and additionally finds that it lacked spontaneity. When asked at the hearing about her practice in Canada, she replied that she had made a phone call to a Canadian sister and was told that it was mysterious, that she should look at the Internet and that there was no gathering place here. The Principal Appellant identified that the website she went to was the Almighty God website. When asked if she did anything else other than visiting the website to practice her faith in Canada, she replied that she did not do anything. The RAD notes that the Principal Appellant did have some knowledge about the Almighty God religion and finds that this would be consistent with visiting the church's website. However, the Principal Appellant provided no information about how she practices the religion other than reading articles and information on the website.

The RAD has considered the lack of details surrounding the Principal Appellant's Canadian practice, along with credibility concerns about her practice of the religion in China, incorrect knowledge of the basic tenant of the faith, and the complete absence of supporting documentation from family, friends or the church contact person in Canada. The RAD finds that the Principal Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, the genuineness of her practice of the Church of Almighty God religion in Canada or in China. Given that the Minor Appellant's claim is based on his mother's religious practice, the RAD agrees with the RPD that the negative credibility findings extend to his claim.

The RAD further finds that the Appellants have not established that they have a sur place claim, given that the extent of the Principal Appellant's involvement in the religion, while in Canada, was looking at the website. There is no evidence in the record that Chinese authorities had any knowledge of her doing this or that there were any repercussions suffered by the Appellants or their family members in China.

Having conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellants have not established that they would face more than a mere possibility of persecution, should they return to China, nor would they be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture. Legal Test

The Appellants argue that the RPD applied the wrong legal test by stating in its reasons that the Appellants had not satisfied their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution. They argue that the correct test is "more than a mere possibility", rather than a "serious possibility". They argue that the RPD used the same test for the section 97 grounds, which was incorrect, as the test for section 97 grounds is higher than that needed for the section 96 grounds.

The RAD finds that the RPD used the correct test when finding that the Appellants had not established a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground if returned to China. The RAD has reviewed Federal Court jurisprudence and finds that the wording "serious possibility" has been endorsed by the Court. Justice Annis concluded in Sivaraththinam that Adjei established the proper expression of the standard to determine a well-founded fear as a "reasonable chance", "reasonable possibility", "serious possibility", or "good grounds". 3

The RAD agrees with the Appellants that the RPD did not articulate the correct test for the section 97 grounds, which should have been "on a balance of probabilities", which is a more stringent test. However, the RAD finds that the failure to state the correct test was not determinative of the claim, which was based on a Convention ground.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
